summary: We have developed an interactive web application that harmonizes satellite data on active fires and visualizes them through a dynamic calendar, tailored specifically for the Huánuco region and the Peruvian Amazon. To address the challenges of environmental monitoring, the platform integrates complex data from sources such as NASA FIRMS, presenting it via an intuitive interface that facilitates the temporal and spatial tracking of fire hotspots in areas with high ecological and agricultural vulnerability. Its significance lies in providing local authorities, communities, and response teams in our region with a vital tool for early prevention, informed decision-making, and the mitigation of the devastating impacts of forest fires on our forests, biodiversity, and local livelihoods.
details:
FireCal is an interactive web application created to monitor, harmonize, and predict wildfire risk using real NASA satellite data, with a primary focus on Huánuco and the Peruvian Amazon, while remaining fully scalable to any country worldwide. Through an intuitive interface that requires no coding skills or specialized GIS software, users can explore thermal hotspots on a map from 2001 to the present, analyze the day-by-day evolution and burned area of individual fires, visualize patterns in an interactive calendar and a monthly statistical table, and project a two-week risk map across grid cells of approximately 11 kilometers.

The platform's core benefit lies in democratizing space science by transforming raw satellite records from NASA FIRMS, GIBS, and POWER into actionable visual alerts with a single click for local authorities, brigades, and communities. To ensure speed and accessibility in areas with limited connectivity, priority regions—including Huánuco, Ucayali, Loreto, Madre de Dios, San Martín, Amazonas, and all of Peru—come preloaded with 25 years of historical data for instant access, optimizing subsequent queries through local browser caching.

In terms of impact, FireCal strengthens early prevention and strategic resource allocation. By concentrating danger alerts within the 15% of the territory facing the highest risk (high and very high levels), it enables preventive patrols to focus directly on the most vulnerable zones ahead of critical burning peaks (such as the July-to-October season in Huánuco). In retrospective validation tests using real data from 2024 and 2025, between 33% and 69% of actual wildfires occurred within that prioritized 15% high-risk area, demonstrating its real-world value in protecting Amazonian biodiversity and local livelihoods.

For development, we used standard web technologies (HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript) runnable directly on modern browsers without expensive backend servers, integrating direct API consumption from NASA (MAP_KEY from FIRMS for active fire detections, GIBS for daily satellite imagery, and POWER for rainfall and humidity variables), alongside interactive mapping libraries and local storage management (LocalStorage) to animate fire progression and export reports in CSV format.

The project's creativity and technical rigor stand out in how it bridges the technological gap between two satellite generations: older MODIS sensors (1 km resolution, since 2000) and modern VIIRS sensors (375 m resolution, since 2012). Because modern sensors detect much smaller fires, FireCal applies a monthly calibration factor derived from overlapping operational years to express 25 years of history on a single comparable scale (cell-days), explaining this methodology visually and interactively to the user. Additionally, it features a historical audit function that allows users to select past dates to verify the predictive model's accuracy against actual historical fires in real time.

Ultimately, the entire design was shaped by local seasonal climate dynamics, NASA server constraints limiting requests to 5-day blocks, and the need to deliver plain-language diagnostics explaining why a zone is at risk and what actions to take—achieving a comprehensive, modular, and scientifically validated solution built by a compact team of two people.
